Biochemical and crystallographic investigations have unveiled the atomic architectures and catalytic profiles of two newly isolated thermophilic sugar aminotransferases, providing structural insights into how these biocatalytic enzymes operate and endure at elevated temperatures. Identified respectively from deep subsurface oil reservoir water and a hydrothermal archaeon, the enzymes SAT4182 and AVTA6 catalyse the first half-reaction of keto-sugar transamination, producing amino-sugars of significant interest to synthetic chemistry and pharmaceutical development. Sugar aminotransferases, abbreviated as SATs, belong to the pyridoxal-5-phosphate-dependent aminotransferase family VI, a group encompassing DegT, DnrJ, EryC1, and StrS enzymes that are phylogenetically divided into three principal subgroups based on substrate regioselectivity. Despite tens of thousands of family VI sequences residing in international protein repositories, only a tiny fraction had previously been biochemically examined, and only a single three-dimensional structure from a thermophilic source had been determined. The structural solutions for SAT4182 and AVTA6, resolved to high resolutions of 1.43 Å and 1.27 Å, now represent only the second and third thermophilic structures solved within this entire family, providing a comparative window into the diverse physical mechanisms that extreme microbes evolve to preserve catalytic machinery under thermal duress.
The two enzymes examined in this investigation trace their origins to divergent thermal environments, illustrating the versatility of environmental genomics and targeted database mining for enzyme discovery. SAT4182 was recovered from microbial biomass collected from one litre of production water sampled at seventy degrees Celsius from the Troll C oil reservoir located in the North Sea. Following total genomic DNA extraction via an amended cetyltrimethylammonium bromide protocol and pyrosequencing, metagenomic assembly identified an open reading frame encoding a 375-amino-acid polypeptide with a predicted molecular mass of approximately 42 kilodaltons, classified as an uncharacterised member of subgroup VIα closely related to Thermoanaerobacter uzonensis. In parallel, AVTA6 was uncovered by querying thermophilic archaeal genomes with the known mesophilic sugar transaminase WecE from Escherichia coli, which identified a 373-amino-acid protein from Archaeoglobus veneficus sharing forty-seven percent sequence identity and belonging to subgroup VIβ. Both sequences featured the four conserved diagnostic sequence motifs flanking the active site that define sugar aminotransferase enzymes. To facilitate controlled laboratory investigation, synthetic codon-optimised genes were cloned into pET21b and pLATE51 expression vectors and transformed into Escherichia coli BL21 DE3 cells, where both recombinant proteins were successfully overexpressed and subsequently purified to homogeneity using nickel affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography.
Hydrodynamic profiling via size-exclusion chromatography highlighted distinctive physical behaviours between the two purified biocatalysts in their solution states. During gel filtration on a Superdex 75 column, SAT4182 eluted at a volume of 63.5 millilitres, an elution volume indicating an apparent hydrodynamic radius substantially smaller than that anticipated for a standard monomer and suggesting an unusually compact, tightly packed tertiary structure. In contrast, AVTA6 eluted from a Superdex 200 column at a volume of 73 millilitres, aligning precisely with the predicted molecular mass of a stable homodimer in solution. Spectrophotometric analyses confirmed that both purified enzymes effectively coordinate their essential pyridoxal-5-phosphate cofactor to assemble an active catalytic centre. Free pyridoxal-5-phosphate in aqueous solution exhibits a characteristic absorbance peak near 390 nanometres, which shifted upon incubation with purified enzyme to a distinct absorbance maximum between 410 and 420 nanometres. This pronounced spectral shift, which took place at ambient room temperature alongside a visible colour transition, confirmed the spontaneous formation of the internal aldimine Schiff base between the cofactor and the conserved catalytic lysine residue situated within each enzyme active site.
Thermal stress assays demonstrated remarkable structural resistance in both enzymes, confirming that their cofactor-binding complexes remain intact well beyond ambient temperatures. When incubated across a temperature gradient extending from 30 °C to 90 °C in ten-degree increments, SAT4182 demonstrated an extraordinarily resilient internal aldimine linkage that remained fully stable up to 90 °C without denaturation or cofactor dissociation. The archaeal enzyme AVTA6 likewise exhibited pronounced thermal resistance, maintaining its intact internal aldimine complex at temperatures up to 80 °C before thermal perturbation compromised cofactor retention. These stability benchmarks demonstrate that the basic folding architecture of each enzyme is inherently adapted to survive environmental temperatures that would rapidly unfold typical mesophilic homologues. The presence of such stable internal aldimine complexes provided an experimental platform to probe how the thermal stability of the structural scaffold correlates with actual catalytic efficiency across varying thermal conditions.
Catalytic activity was evaluated by measuring the ability of each enzyme to execute the initial half-reaction of the transamination cycle, specifically the deamination of an amino donor to generate pyridoxamine phosphate, designated PMP. During transamination, the internal aldimine formed between the enzyme catalytic lysine and pyridoxal-5-phosphate is exchanged for an incoming amino acid donor to assemble an external aldimine, which undergoes proton abstraction, quinonoid formation, and subsequent hydrolysis to yield an alpha-keto acid and enzyme-bound PMP. When incubated with L-glutamate in a reaction buffer containing 50 millimolar HEPES at pH 8.0 and 500 millimolar sodium chloride, both enzymes induced a rapid loss of absorbance at 420 nanometres and a concomitant emergence of an absorbance peak at 320 to 330 nanometres. This clear spectral transformation directly established the production of PMP and the disruption of the resting internal aldimine linkage. Calculating the integrated area under the curve across the 300 to 340 nanometre interval confirmed that both SAT4182 and AVTA6 successfully execute this half-reaction, converting L-glutamate into alpha-ketoglutarate while priming the cofactor for subsequent sugar amination.
Systematic substrate screening across twelve distinct L-amino acids revealed unexpected differences in donor specificity between the two enzymes, challenging conventional assumptions regarding the narrow donor selectivity of sugar aminotransferases. Assaying the panel using GraphPad Prism trapezoidal integration of PMP formation and aldimine depletion showed that SAT4182 accepts three distinct amino acid donors. L-glutamate supported the greatest conversion, yielding an integrated PMP production area of 7.31 ± 0.11 arbitrary absorbance units multiplied by nanometres, accompanied by an aldimine depletion of 1.23 ± 0.07. L-serine served as an effective alternative donor, producing 6.74 ± 0.11 AU·nm of PMP with a depletion value of 1.25 ± 0.003, whereas L-histidine supported detectable conversion with 6.46 ± 0.14 AU·nm of PMP, albeit with lower aldimine depletion measuring 0.60 ± 0.01. By comparison, AVTA6 demonstrated a more restricted profile, utilising only two acidic amino acids. L-glutamate functioned as the preferred substrate, generating 6.61 ± 0.18 AU·nm of PMP with 0.43 ± 0.16 AU·nm depletion, while L-aspartate was processed with moderate efficiency, producing 5.75 ± 0.11 AU·nm of PMP while largely retaining its aldimine absorbance signal at 1.48 ± 0.16 AU·nm.
The thermal boundaries governing catalytic turnover diverged notably from structural unfolding limits, underscoring fundamental differences between structural survival and catalytic viability. When tested following a defined thirty-minute thermal stress across a range from 30 °C to 90 °C, SAT4182 displayed zero detectable PMP generation below 50 °C, demonstrating that it is an obligate thermophile that requires elevated thermal energy to overcome activation barriers and perform catalysis. SAT4182 operated efficiently throughout a working window of 50 °C to 70 °C, generating integrated PMP values of 4.33 to 5.55 AU·nm, but experienced a total collapse of catalytic turnover at temperatures above 70 °C, even though its internal aldimine scaffold remained physically stable up to 90 °C. Conversely, AVTA6 demonstrated a broader catalytic window, executing detectable deamination at 30 °C and retaining steady catalytic activity across the entire range from 30 °C to 80 °C, with PMP production areas between 4.61 and 5.56 AU·nm before losing activity at 90 °C. The loss of catalytic competence in SAT4182 above 70 °C, despite preserving its overall tertiary fold, indicates that thermal motion at elevated temperatures alters active-site geometry, whereas the active centre of AVTA6 remains catalytically competent up to its structural threshold.
Synchrotron X-ray crystallographic data collected at Diamond Light Source enabled the determination of the atomic structures of both biocatalysts, establishing their placement within the classical aspartate aminotransferase type I fold superfamily. SAT4182 crystallised in the trigonal space group P3221 and was refined to 1.43 Å resolution with Rwork and Rfree values of 0.167 and 0.198, with its crystallographic asymmetric unit containing a single protein monomer of 369 ordered residues. AVTA6 crystallised in the orthorhombic space group P212121 and was resolved to 1.27 Å resolution with Rwork and Rfree values of 0.153 and 0.177, containing two monomers comprising 736 residues within the asymmetric unit. In both enzymes, the protomer architecture is organised around a dominant cofactor-binding central domain featuring a seven-stranded beta-sheet flanked on both sides by alpha-helices, bounded by smaller flanking N- and C-terminal segments. Although the asymmetric unit of SAT4182 contained a monomer, biological assembly analysis verified that it functions as a dimer, mirroring the crystallographic dimer seen in AVTA6. Superimposing the two functional dimers revealed an overall root-mean-square deviation of 1.105 Å across 500 equivalent alpha-carbon positions, confirming strong conservation of the global quaternary architecture.
Inspection of the crystallographic models confirmed that both enzymes complete functional catalytic centres at their dimer interfaces via reciprocal interactions from adjoining subunits. The pyridoxal-5-phosphate cofactor forms a covalent internal aldimine Schiff base with a conserved active-site residue, identified as Lys183 in SAT4182 and Lys185 in AVTA6, while the pyridine ring nitrogen atom establishes a hydrogen bond with an invariant acidic anchor, Asp154 in SAT4182 and Asp156 in AVTA6. In SAT4182, the cofactor phosphate moiety is coordinated by hydrogen bonds from Gly57, Thr58, Ser178, and Asn180, alongside water-mediated bridges through Gln55 and Gly190, with hydrophobic contacts supplied by Phe83 and Val128. Critical cross-subunit contributions are provided by Gln210, Asn226, and Arg228 from the partner monomer. In AVTA6, phosphate coordination is maintained by Gly59, Ser60, Ser180, Phe85, and Tyr182, with bridging interactions from Pro183, Arg252, and Tyr309, and partner chain contributions from Tyr213 and Asn227. Crucially, AVTA6 features a deeper, more enclosed active-site cavity, whereas SAT4182 displays a wider, more accessible pocket lined by aromatic residues Trp282 and Phe315. In addition, SAT4182 incorporates a charged Glu157 residue that is replaced by a neutral Gln159 in AVTA6, a chemical divergence that alters local electrostatic charge and likely dictates whether C4-keto or C3-keto sugars and specific amino acid donors can be accommodated.
Quantitative computational evaluation of the structural models explained how each thermophilic enzyme achieves extreme resilience through distinct physical mechanisms compared to the mesophilic counterpart WecE from Escherichia coli. In SAT4182, thermal stabilisation is driven primarily by an extensive ionic network, boasting 63 salt bridges per monomer compared to 46 in mesophilic WecE, alongside a highly negative folding free energy of −367.63 kilocalories per mole, which deviates by −19.33 kcal/mol from expected values. Packing defects in SAT4182 were restricted to 29, closely matching the ideal theoretical value of 25 while outperforming the 83 defects observed in WecE. In contrast, AVTA6 incorporates 57 salt bridges per monomer but uniquely possesses an internal covalent brace in the form of an intrachain disulphide bond between Cys301 and Cys358 that links alpha-helices 9 and 11, a feature absent in both SAT4182 and WecE. This covalent cross-link provides structural rigidity to the catalytic pocket at extreme temperatures, explaining why AVTA6 retains deamination capacity up to 80 °C. The authors emphasise that while both enzymes effectively drive the first half of the transamination cycle, complete catalytic turnover awaits future identification of their physiological nucleotide-diphosphate-keto-sugar acceptors, as candidate substrates dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose and dGDP-4-keto-6-deoxymannose failed to regenerate pyridoxal-5-phosphate in exploratory trials.

Safety Guidelines
1. Lightning is dangerous and can cause serious harm to human and animal lives, electricity and communication networks, and household appliances connected to electrical conductors. The public is advised to take the following precautions as soon as dark clouds begin to appear. Since lightning may not always be visible, these precautions should not be ignored.
2. Move indoors immediately at the first sign of lightning. Staying in open spaces increases the risk of being struck.
3. Keep doors and windows closed when strong winds and lightning are expected. Avoid standing near doors and windows. Stay inside buildings and minimise contact with walls and floors.
4. Disconnect electrical appliances from power sources and avoid contact with electrical equipment during lightning.
5. Avoid using landline telephones during lightning. Mobile phone use is considered safe.
6. Avoid playing in open spaces or on terraces, including for children, when the sky is overcast.
7. Do not stand under trees during lightning or park vehicles beneath them.
8. Remain inside vehicles during lightning and keep your hands and feet inside. Avoid travelling on bicycles, motorcycles and tractors. Take shelter in a safe building until the lightning subsides.
9. Do not go to terraces or open courtyards to collect clothes when lightning is occurring.
10. Secure objects that could be blown away or toppled by strong winds.
11. Avoid bathing or collecting water from taps during lightning, as electricity may travel through water pipes.
12. Do not enter water bodies to fish or bathe during lightning. Stop fishing, boating and other water-based activities as soon as dark clouds appear and head towards the nearest shore. Do not stand on boat decks, cast fishing lines or throw nets during lightning.
13. Avoid flying kites.
14. Do not sit on terraces, elevated places or tree branches during lightning.
15. Do not tether domestic animals in open areas during such conditions. Avoid going outside to untie or relocate them after dark clouds appear, as this could expose you to lightning.
16. If caught in an open area with no access to a nearby building, keep your feet together, tuck your head between your knees and crouch in a ball-like position.
17. Lightning arresters can be installed on buildings to provide protection against lightning strikes. Surge protectors can also be fitted to safeguard electrical appliances.
18. A lightning strike can cause burns, loss of vision or hearing, and even cardiac arrest. A person struck by lightning does not retain an electrical charge, so it is safe to provide first aid. The first 30 seconds after a lightning strike are crucial for saving a life. Ensure that the affected person receives medical assistance immediately.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” M365 Core President Jason Henderson said the following day in a memo sent to staff seen by Reuters. The exec added that he oversaw an in-depth review of the structural issues that made this widespread outage possible.
Microsoft previously explained that the outage was caused by “an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” with no relation to cyberattacks or AI systems. “In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” he wrote.

If the timing couldn’t be worse, Microsoft now seems determined to make all the required changes to restore services affected by major failures in under an hour.
“Our work doesn’t end when service is restored. Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority,” a company spokesperson told Reuters.
